title: Binary Search Trees: Delete
oneLiner: Three cases, one for each possible number of children the node being removed has.
keyTakeaway: Deleting a leaf or a one-child node is easy (remove it, or splice its child into its spot). Deleting a node with TWO children is the hard case, solved by not actually deleting it: copy in its inorder successor's value (the smallest value in its right subtree), then delete THAT successor instead -- which is guaranteed to have at most one child, reducing back to an easy case.
explanation: Find the node first, using the same left/right walk as Search. Once found, there are exactly three shapes it can be in: NO children (a leaf) -- just remove it, nothing to reconnect. ONE child -- splice that child directly into the removed node's spot (the parent now points at the grandchild). TWO children -- this is the case that needs a trick, because there's no single child to promote without breaking the BST property. The fix: find the inorder SUCCESSOR (the smallest value in the right subtree -- keep walking left from root.Right until there's no more left), copy that successor's VALUE into the node being "deleted" (the node itself never actually moves), then recursively delete the successor from the right subtree. The successor is guaranteed to have no left child (that's what made it the smallest), so deleting it is always one of the two easy cases -- the hard case reduces itself to an easy one instead of needing its own separate logic. Watch out for forgetting to RECONNECT the result of each recursive call back to the parent's Left/Right pointer -- deletion has to rebuild the path back up, not just find and detach the target node.

visualizationSteps.message: Deleting 3. Found it at this node -- it has TWO children, the hard case.
Find the inorder successor: walk into the right subtree (4), then keep going left. It has no left child, so 4 IS the successor.
Copy the successor's value (4) onto the node being deleted -- 3 is gone from this spot, replaced by 4.
Now delete the successor's original node (4) from the right subtree -- it was a leaf, so this is the easy "no children" case. Done.

complexity.note: DeleteAndVerify builds the tree from the n values (n inserts at up to h steps each, O(n · h): O(n log n) balanced, O(n²) for sorted input), deletes one key and then reads the tree back in order (O(n)). The build dominates. The delete itself is O(h): one path down to find the node, then possibly another down to its successor. Space is O(n) for the tree and the in-order output, plus O(h) recursion.
